provenance: Ibn al-Laḥḥām's furūʿ under qawāʿid 43 (the command) and 61 (wording vs occasion) annotated by an LLM agent against the M5 readings in Usul.Dalala; claims checked by Lean (UsulTest/Takhrij.lean); awaiting human review (Review.tla).

cases.note: Whether writing or gesture counts as a command (al-Qadi: not truly; his Jami' argument from the Prophet's letters implies it does) is a question about what constitutes the command, prior to and outside the kernel, which presupposes a command and only assigns its status.

Whether it is proper to ask of a bare command 'is it obligatory?' is a dialectical point on which Abu Ya'la reports only refusal and concession; it is one of the text's 'fawa'id usuliyya', not a case whose ruling could be tested.

Whether the Prophet's act is called a command literally (Abu al-Barakat: only figuratively, per Ahmad and the majority; some Malikis/Shafi'is and Abu Ya'la's Kifaya: literally) is governed by the theory of the Prophet's acts and the semantics of the word 'amr', not by the bare-command default.

Whether an unqualified threat, or the words 'obligatory'/'fard', are a text (nass) for obligation that admits no reinterpretation (al-Qadi: no; Abu al-Barakat, preferred: yes) asks whether an indication may override the default at all, whereas the kernel lets any qarina override every command.

When an indication only removes obligation without fixing another status, some Hanafis/Shafi'is (al-Razi) let the command still prove recommendation or permission while Abu Ya'la's report, Ibn Burhan, Abu al-Tayyib and al-Tamimi deny it (two wujuh for the Hanbalis per Abu al-Khattab); the kernel's qarina always names the target status, so it cannot express a merely negating indication.

A command whose object is partly obligatory and partly recommended ('do good', 'leave what makes you doubt') is read by Abu al-'Abbas as meaning the obligatory in the obligatory items and the recommended in the recommended ones, which needs a status per covered item, while the encoder takes one qarina for one act.

Once nadb (or ibaha) is meant by the command the status is not in dispute; the dispute (literal per Ahmad's apparent words, al-Qadi and most companions vs figurative per al-Karkhi, al-Razi and al-Halwani; for ibaha Abu al-Barakat and Ibn 'Aqil say figurative) is over literal vs figurative usage, which the kernel does not model.

Breaking the fast is better for every traveller, with or without hardship, by the general wording 'it is not piety to fast while travelling' (a verbal sentence, indefinite under negation): a traveller without hardship is outside the occasion but covered by the general wording.

An animal slaughtered without tasmiya is unlawful (al-sahih of the madhhab) by the general wording of 'do not eat of that over which God's name has not been mentioned', applied beyond its occasion; the contrary view implied by 'al-sahih' is not stated here (the text defers to its discussion of the basmala).

The 'araya licence does not cover a buyer without need, which looks like an exception to the generality of the definite article, but Ibn al-Lahham resolves it by reading 'al-'araya' as the known ('ahdi) sale licensed for the needy, so the wording is not general and a non-needy buyer, outside the occasion, is not covered.
